Someone told me recently that p(Doom)1 looks too AI-generated. They were right, and the honest response isn't a promise to do better; it's showing the work.

This week I sat down with 470 generated art assets and judged every one of them in 23 minutes. About one decision every three seconds. 274 discarded, 197 kept.

The kept ones aren't the interesting part. These are some of the discards, in the notes I typed at the time:

"Not nuclear symbol. Experiment with new, geometric abstract representation of doom escalation."

"Not a lock. Try a more symbolic representation in the abstract. Consider an alien culture's representation of safe."

"silhouette too obviously male, too obviously signalling Operator" - written three times, against three different versions, because they kept arriving that way.

"this does not reflect what things do in reality and is distressing to look at"

"one red team one blue team, combat, not chess; can be engineers facing each other off"

"we seem to have massively overindexed on the banker's lamp as an art asset"

And my favourite, which I stand by: "I have no idea what this is for and will watch out for it."

The review tool logs every change of mind rather than overwriting it, which turned out to matter on day one: one asset went remix, remix, remix, remix, remix, and then keep. Twelve assets had their verdict reversed mid-session. Under the old design all of that would have been silently overwritten by the last click.

Generated art is a placeholder. It is a fast way to find out what you actually want, and the finding-out is done by throwing most of it away and being able to say why. That taste is the part that doesn't come out of a model, and it's what the funding is for.

p(Doom)1 is a game about the people trying to stop AI going badly wrong. You can't win; you can only buy time.

copy.devlog_long:
# 274 of 470

The only public criticism this project has had is that the art looks too AI-generated. It does. Here is what I did about it, and why the discards are the interesting half.

On Friday I judged 470 generated assets in 23 minutes - about one decision every 2.9 seconds. 274 discarded, 197 kept, and 320 notes typed in the gaps.

## The notes

> "Not nuclear symbol. Experiment with new, geometric abstract representation of doom escalation"

> "Not a lock. Try a more symbolic representation in the abstract. Consider an alien culture's representation of safe."

> "this is dangerously close to an mtg symbol. think about better representation for emotional burnout"

> "poorly articulated design keeps leaning to weird buildings interpolating into each other destructively"

> "this does not reflect what things do in reality and is distressing to look at"

> "one red team one blue team, combat, not chess; can be engineers facing each other off"

> "eyes have too much definition, breaks immersion"

> "we seem to have massively overindexed on the banker's lamp as an art asset"

> "I have no idea what this is for and will watch out for it"

Three separate versions of a founder silhouette were rejected with the same sentence: *too obviously male, too obviously signalling Operator*. That is not a rendering problem; it is a design problem the generator could not have known it had.

One note is a keep, and it is the one that changed the most downstream: *"This being on a lanyard is amazing. Consider us using this in other employee_role icons. Consider propagating this up into design documents."* A single accessory, spotted in three seconds, became a rule for a whole icon family.

## What the log caught

The review tool appends every judgement rather than overwriting the last one. That decision landed about four hours before it was needed.

Twelve assets had their verdict reversed mid-session. One went remix, remix, remix, remix, remix, keep. Another went shelf, keep. Another went keep, discard. Under a plain state file every one of those earlier judgements would have been gone, and the record would have shown a confident single verdict that was never how it happened.

## What it measured about the tool, not the art

The morning of the review I had designed a two-axis model with a *harvest* tag, for assets that were wrong overall but had a good corner worth keeping. In the first real session it was used zero times. Zero shelf verdicts survived either.

At 2.9 seconds an asset there is no room to type a tag. It was a slow-lane feature offered in a fast lane, and the measurement contradicts the design intent from that same morning. I would rather write that down than quietly drop it.

## Why any of this matters

Generated art is a placeholder, and a useful one: it is a fast way to find out what you actually want. But the finding-out happens by throwing most of it away and being able to say why, in specific words, quickly. That is taste, it is the part that does not come out of a model, and it is what the funding is for.

p(Doom)1 is a game about the people trying to stop AI from going badly wrong. You cannot win; you can only buy time. The minimum funding round closes 9 September.

[Play it](https://pdoom1.com/?utm_source=devlog&utm_medium=owned&utm_campaign=art-cull-2026-08) - [back it](https://manifund.org/projects/fund-development-of-pdoom1)
